posts.snippet:
OpenAI just released their official security scanner: `openai/codex-security` — an open-source CLI & TypeScript SDK for AI-assisted vulnerability scanning and threat modeling.

While build-time scanning (SAST/DAST) is vital for identifying code-level flaws, cybersecurity architects face a far bigger challenge in 2026:

👉 **What happens at RUNTIME when a compromised AI Agent holds live OAuth tokens and enterprise API access?**

Static scanning tools and LLM prompt firewalls operate on semantic probabilities. If an agent is hijacked via Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) during real-time execution, build-time code scanners become completely transparent.

This is precisely the gap we address with **DROS-VEP-lite**.

While OpenAI's tool secures the development boundary (Build-Time), DROS enforces a **<500ns deterministic binary circuit breaker at the C-ABI (Application Binary Interface) system call layer (Runtime)**:

1. **Build-Time vs. Runtime:** Scanning code before deployment vs. enforcing mathematical-grade bounds on live tool calls.
2. **Context Loss Resolution:** Utilizing 3-tier PKI certificate identity binding (DIT Tokens) so the GuardVM recognizes agent identities beneath generic OS runtime processes.
3. **Zero Semantic Dependencies:** Permitted operations are pre-compiled into immutable O(1) bitmaps — if the policy bit is 0, the syscall physically fails regardless of prompt manipulation.

OpenAI is advancing static code defense, and DROS is building the deterministic execution control plane for the Agentic Web!

📄 New report. Familiar challenge.
A newly published report by Strider Technologies, "Contested Ground – Russia's Parallel Engagement in India and the Risks to Europe's Economic Security", highlights a reality that many export control professionals have been observing for some time.

The report does not argue that Europe should disengage from India.
Instead, it makes a more nuanced point:
As Europe deepens its economic and technological cooperation with India, companies must also understand the parallel strategic activities taking place in the same ecosystem.

Among the risks identified are:
✅ diversion of dual-use goods through complex supply chains
✅ sanctions circumvention using third-country intermediaries
✅ technology leakage within shared industrial ecosystems
✅ research collaboration and talent spillover
In other words...
The challenge is no longer simply "Is this export compliant?"
The real question becomes:
"What is happening around my products, my suppliers, my customers, my partners and my technology?"

That is precisely why I believe Export Control must evolve from a purely compliance function into an intelligence function.
Traditional compliance checks a transaction.
Export Control Intelligence continuously monitors the environment in which that transaction takes place.
It connects:
• geopolitical developments
• sanctions
• product classifications
• supply-chain intelligence
• ownership structures
• end-use risks
• diversion patterns
• adverse media
• regulatory developments
...to provide organisations with the context needed to make better decisions before risks materialise.

This philosophy is at the heart of WZ52.
Rather than treating export control as a series of isolated compliance checks, WZ52 is being developed as an Export Control Intelligence platform, combining compliance workflows with continuous intelligence, risk monitoring and decision support.

As global supply chains become more complex, compliance alone is unlikely to be sufficient.
Compliance checks. Intelligence understands.

The Illusion of Absolute Neutrality: What the Tech World Can Learn from Pavel Durov

From the outside, building a platform used by a billion people looks like the ultimate tech success story. High valuation, massive scale, and total independence.
But recent geopolitical events surrounding Telegram highlight a complex reality that every founder, architect, and tech leader must eventually face: Scale changes the rules of engagement.
When a platform evolves from a simple messaging tool into a global communications and financial infrastructure, it inevitably collides with nation-states.
Here are three key takeaways for the tech industry:
1. Neutrality is no longer a passive stance Building a platform with minimal moderation in the name of privacy is a noble engineering ethos. However, in a hyper-polarized world, absolute neutrality is often perceived by regulators as non-compliance. Being "for everyone" can quickly make you target number one for every jurisdiction.
2. Decentralize the responsibility, not just the code When a global platform's identity, vision, and operational authority are heavily tied to a single founder, that individual becomes a single point of failure. Modern tech governance requires distributing leadership and regulatory frameworks just as rigorously as we distribute database workloads.
3. The balancing act of privacy vs. compliance The boundary between protecting user privacy and preventing criminal misuse remains one of tech's hardest unsolved problems. There are no easy architectural fixes here—only trade-offs between user trust, legal exposure, and platform integrity.
Success in tech today isn't just about elegant code or exponential user growth—it’s about navigating the complex intersection of technology, law, and global politics.
How do you see the future of tech regulation evolving? Can privacy-first platforms survive without compromising their core principles?

For years, the conversation has been, "What new tool should we add?"

Law firms have invested heavily in best-of-breed software:
• Case management
• Intake
• Marketing
• AI assistants
• Phone systems
• Document automation
• Medical record retrieval
• Reporting
• Client communication

Each solved a specific problem.

But together, they've created something else: Complexity.

Every new platform introduces another login, another integration, another training process, another vendor relationship, and another data silo.

I believe the next competitive advantage won't come from having the most technology.

It will come from having the fewest platforms needed to deliver the best client experience.

We're already seeing AI blur the lines between categories. Features that once required standalone products are becoming embedded into existing platforms. 

Vendors are expanding beyond their original purpose, and firms are beginning to ask whether they need ten different systems—or five.

Consolidation isn't just about reducing software costs.
-It's about reducing friction.
-Less context switching.
-Less duplicate data.
-Less time spent managing technology.
-More time serving clients.

I'm curious whether others are seeing the same trend.

Are law firms entering an era of tech expansion... or tech consolidation?

💡 Can European Patent Attorneys Reduce Costs Without Compromising Quality? Absolutely.

One of the most effective ways to improve efficiency is by outsourcing technical patent work to experienced Indian IP professionals while retaining all strategic and legal decision-making in Europe.

Why does this model work so well?

Because the Indian Patents Act, 1970 and the European Patent Convention (EPC) share the same core patentability principles:

✅ Novelty
✅ Inventive Step (Non-obviousness)
✅ Industrial Applicability
✅ Sufficiency of Disclosure
✅ Unity of Invention
✅ Claim Support & Specification Requirements

This means that a technically sound first draft or patent analysis prepared in India can often be efficiently reviewed and refined by a European Patent Attorney.

🔹 High-value tasks that can be outsourced include:
• Patentability Searches
• Prior Art Searches
• Freedom-to-Operate (FTO) Analysis
• Patent Landscape Studies
• Patent Drafting (First Drafts)
• Office Action Response Drafts
• Claim Mapping & Claim Charts
• Patent Invalidation Searches
• Design-Around Studies
• Competitor Patent Monitoring
• Scientific & Technical Literature Reviews

📈 Benefits for European Patent Firms

✔ Reduced operational costs
✔ Faster turnaround through time-zone advantage
✔ Access to highly qualified chemistry, pharmaceutical, biotech, and engineering professionals
✔ Increased capacity without expanding in-house teams
✔ More time to focus on legal strategy, client advisory, and EPO proceedings

Of course, legal strategy, prosecution decisions, EPO-specific practice, oral proceedings, and client representation remain with the European Patent Attorney.

The Sixth Anti-Money Laundering Directive (6AMLD) may not apply until July 2027, but the firms that start planning now will be the ones that aren't scrambling later.

Our latest insight from Robbie Cullen breaks down what the 6AMLD means in practice, and why treating it as part of a single AML programme (alongside AMLR and AMLA) matters more than tackling it in isolation.

Key areas firms should be considering now:
🔹Beneficial ownership transparency, including new scope for cryptoasset accounts and wallets.
🔹Expanded account registries and cross-border information sharing.
🔹A more formal, risk-based approach to AML/CTF controls Closer supervisory scrutiny of senior management fitness and propriety.

With transposition due by 10 July 2027, the window to review policies, upgrade systems and embed governance is 2026–2027. Firms operating across multiple EU jurisdictions have the most to gain from a joined-up approach.

posts.title: Stablecoins: moving from trading tool to financial infrastructure
posts.author: Syed Musheer Ahmed
posts.snippet:
Stablecoins: moving from trading tool to financial infrastructure 

Blockchain.com’s State of Stablecoins report studied 57 projects and collected over 1,600 data points across 44 categories. 

Key Highlights: 

📊  The category is growing quickly: The report identified 23 live stablecoins and 34 pre-launch projects. Active projects had risen sharply over the prior 12 to 18 months, with more than a dozen teams planning launches soon. 

🏦 Asset-backed models dominate: 77% of the sample used asset-backed designs (primarily fiat), while 23% were algorithmic. Among asset-backed stablecoins, on-chain collateral represented 54% and off-chain collateral 46%. The US dollar was the main peg, used by 66% of projects. 

📈 Adoption is real, but concentrated: Stablecoins accounted for about $3bn in market value, around 1.5% of total cryptoasset market value. Tether made up 93% of stablecoin market value and roughly 98% of daily stablecoin trading volume. 

🌐 Distribution matters: Stablecoins were listed on more than 50 exchanges. Tether had at least 46 listings, while ten live stablecoins had one or more Tier-1 exchange listings. Liquidity and access were becoming moats. 

⚙️ Ethereum had the lead: #Ethereum was the most widely used layer 1, although fewer than two thirds of projects were building exclusively on it. Bitcoin, NEO and Stellar also appeared across multiple projects. 

💰 Capital was flowing in: Stablecoin teams had raised about $350m in venture funding. Algorithmic stablecoins attracted $174m, traditional asset-backed projects raised $144m, and #crypto-collateralised projects raised $33m. 

⚖️ Regulation was central: Projects were spread across jurisdictions, led by the US and Switzerland. The report flags securities laws, money transmission rules, AML requirements and possible central bank responses as key areas to watch. 

⏭️ The bigger point: stablecoins expand what cryptoassets can do. If volatility is one of the main barriers to broader adoption, stablecoins address a basic market need. Payments, #remittances, lending, derivatives, smart insurance, dApps and treasury management become more practical when the unit of account is stable. 

While no perfect design exists as such, each model carries trade-offs around trust, transparency, scalability, decentralisation and regulation. In the short to medium term, the market may continue to use/rely on the main 5 to 8 significant stablecoins. 

While Stablecoins started primarily to facilitate a trading, the much larger opportunity will be as transaction rails for capital markets and financial infrastructure. 

Where do you think stablecoins will create the most value: #trading, #payments, #treasury, lending, or broader financial market infrastructure? 

FinStep Asia Douglas Arner Sean Lee Angelina Alex Medana Kristi L Swartz Ronit Ghose Monica Jasuja Richard Turrin Dr. Efi Pylarinou Dr. Martha Boeckenfeld Sam Boboev
posts.reason: Detailed stablecoin market and regulation overview with real data; useful context but no immediate call to action for our core buyer segments.

comments.text: The regulatory point buried in there is the real story - stablecoin issuers keep tripping over the line between an e-money token and an asset-referenced token under MiCAR, and the disclosure and reserve requirements differ meaningfully depending on which side of that line they fall.

With Tether still dominating both market value and volume, does the report say anything about how EU-facing distribution is shifting now that non-MiCAR-compliant stablecoins can't be marketed to EU consumers?

We've reviewed a fair number of stablecoin white papers this year, and the algorithmic-versus-asset-backed classification question is exactly where issuers underestimate how much documentation MiCAR expects before they can even talk to a regulator.

posts.title: Participating in the Joint Research Seminar on AI Governance for Sustainable Development: International Law, Climate Responsibility and Technology Regulation, co-organised by the N
posts.author: Pamela Victor-Ibitamuno
posts.snippet:
Participating in the Joint Research Seminar on AI Governance for Sustainable Development: International Law, Climate Responsibility and Technology Regulation, co-organised by the NUS Centre for International Law and the Durham Centre for Sustainable Development Law and Policy (CSDLP) with support from the UNESCO Chair on Artificial Intelligence Law & Sustainability, provided me an opportunity to engage with some of the most pressing questions shaping AI.
 
Professor Petra Minnerop, opened the seminar, setting the stage for a discussion that moved well beyond the usual "AI ethics" framing into harder questions of accountability and equity in governance.

Dr. Jon Truby presented the work of the UNESCO Chair, arguing that the Global South must be an active participant in shaping AI strategy rather than a downstream recipient of standards set by the Global North. 

It was emphasised that AI systems should be viewed through a full life-cycle lens, so that sustainability is built in from the outset rather than retrofitted after deployment. That distinction matters. Post-deployment sustainability measures address symptoms, while life-cycle governance addresses the design choices that create the environmental and social costs in the first place.

Dr Mauricio Figueroa built on this by examining the environmental costs that often go unpriced in AI deployment. His call to treat data centres as industrial infrastructure, rather than abstract "cloud" capacity, is a useful corrective. It reframes AI's environmental footprint in terms already familiar to environmental law. Which I believe makes it far easier to hold providers accountable under existing regulatory tools.

Dr Barry Solaiman, outlined the phases of AI regulation in medical law and raised a point that deserves more attention than it typically gets: local startups building AI-driven medical products frequently struggle to reach hospitals in their own countries because they lack FDA clearance. 

Most countries don't have an equivalent regulatory body of their own. The effect is a de facto market barrier that has little to do with product safety or efficacy and everything to do with regulatory infrastructure. Large incumbents, who can absorb the cost of navigating established regulatory regimes, gain a structural advantage, while local and indigenous innovators are locked out of markets they are best positioned to serve. This is worth flagging as a genuine governance gap, not just a market inefficiency.

Rebecca Owens, PhD  examined the EU AI Act through the lens of the UN SDGs, identifying where the regulation's risk-based approach aligns with sustainable development goals and where it falls short, particularly on questions the Act treats as secondary but the SDGs treat as central.

It was a pleasure to also exchange ideas with Kaspar Rosager Ludvigsen on the sidelines.

posts.title: The CGA has published new rules for licensed operators who accept crypto, and the message is simple: if players are paying you in crypto, you have to actually understand what's com
posts.author: Alex Markides
posts.snippet:
The CGA has published new rules for licensed operators who accept crypto, and the message is simple: if players are paying you in crypto, you have to actually understand what's coming through your doors.

What that means in practice:

You have to know where the money came from. No more accepting a deposit and not looking at it. Operators now need to trace wallets and transactions and screen out anything tied to sanctions, fraud, or mixers (services that hide the origin of funds). You can hire specialists to do the checking but you can't just look away and call it someone else's problem.

Some crypto is simply off the table. Money from sanctioned wallets or mixers is a hard no and are 'expressly prohibited'. Privacy coins built to be untraceable, sketchy meme coins, and wrapped tokens nobody can vouch for are heavily restricted. Boring, traceable stablecoins are the preferred choice. 

Gambling sites are not banks. You can take crypto as payment for gambling. That's it. No swapping coins for players, no exchange services, no acting like a wallet provider. And players can't send crypto to each other on the platform.

Keep the money tidy and separate. Player funds in one place, company funds in another, everything recorded so it holds up to an audit. No personal or owners' wallets in the mix.

The line that ties it all together: you can outsource the work, but you can't outsource the responsibility. If something goes wrong, it's still on the license holder.

There's a clock on this too. Some bans apply now (e.g., sanctioned wallets, mixers etc). A written policy is due to the CGA by September 2026. Everything fully built and running by June 2027.

If you're licensed in Curaçao and crypto is a real part of your payment mix, this is worth starting on now rather than the week before the deadline.

Better information leads to better leadership. It helps us make stronger strategic decisions, create more empathetic workplaces, and serve our clients with greater insight.

Maybe it’s time we stop treating money as a taboo topic and start treating it as a leadership conversation.

posts.title: Unpopular opinion: MiCA didn't kill European crypto. It killed the excuse not to build like it mattered.
posts.author: Artem Zaitsev
posts.snippet:
Unpopular opinion: MiCA didn't kill European crypto. It killed the excuse not to build like it mattered.

I get the case against it. Compliance reviews that used to take an afternoon now take weeks. A small team pays the same legal overhead as a company ten times its size, which is a real moat for whoever already had a compliance department. A few projects pulled out of the EU rather than deal with it. None of that is imaginary.

But the case for it is stronger than most builders admit in private. Before MiCA, "compliant" meant whatever a given country's regulator felt like that year. One licence, passportable across the whole EU, is the kind of certainty that finally let banks and asset managers touch crypto rails without their legal team walking out. That's not nothing.

Here's where I land: the law was never the problem. The problem was that most teams had never treated regulatory state as part of the product. It lived in a spreadsheet, or in someone's head, or nowhere. MiCA just made that debt due all at once.

I'd rather build in one market with a strict rulebook than in ten markets each guessing at their own.

Banka mevduatı, altın hesabı, kiralık kasa ve kripto varlıklar ise tek cümlelik bir kalıpla koruma dışında bırakılıyor: "ölçülülük ilkesi gereği." Üstelik tedbir konulmayan hesaplar için bankalara döküm müzekkeresi yazılması, mal kaçırmayı önleyen bir araç olmaktan çıkıp onu tetikleyen bir erken uyarıya dönüşebiliyor.

Ortaya bir paradoks çıkıyor: Üzerine taşınmaz kayıtlı görünen ama tek kuruş nakde erişemeyen eş, kâğıt üzerinde "varlıklı" sayılıp korumasız kalıyor. Bedeli ödeyen hep aynı kişi: üzerine tek bir mal kayıtlı olmayan eş ve çocukları.
Kişisel Görüşüm serisinin bu yazısında, sakıncalı bulduğum bu uygulama kalıbını, görünmeyen sonuçlarını ve mahkemelere, kanun koyucuya ve meslektaşlarıma yönelik somut önerilerimi ele aldım. Görüşlerinizi ve sorularınızı memnuniyetle beklerim; mesaj kutum açık.
Ekteki belgede makalenin önce Türkçe, ardından İngilizce tam metni yer almaktadır. (İngilizce metin 9. sayfadan itibaren başlar.)
⸻
A MILLION-LIRA JUDGMENT, AN EMPTY ACCOUNT: WHO DO THESE INJUNCTIONS PROTECT?

In divorce and matrimonial property cases, interim injunctions are often limited to land and vehicle registries. Bank deposits, gold accounts, safe-deposit boxes and crypto assets are carved out with a single boilerplate phrase: "pursuant to the principle of proportionality." Worse, requesting bank statements for accounts that were not frozen can turn the court's inquiry from a safeguard into an early warning that triggers the very dissipation it should prevent.
The consequences form a chain: maintenance whose source is unprotected exists only on paper; damages judgments are enforced against long-emptied accounts; and legal aid is locked to a headman's poverty certificate. A paradox emerges: a spouse with property on record but no access to a single lira of cash is deemed "wealthy" on paper and left without protection. The price is paid, every time, by the same person: the spouse with no assets in her name, and her children.
In this Personal Opinion piece, I set out why I find this pattern harmful, its invisible consequences, and my concrete recommendations to courts, to the legislator and to colleagues. Comments and questions are most welcome; my inbox is open.

Azrin was Acting Head of Procurement at Labuan Shipyard & Engineering Sdn Bhd.

9 years and 2 months of service.

Then 2 things landed on his desk. A pricing form with a number that didn't add up. And vendor quotes that weren't real.

He told the court he didn't know. The Industrial Court didn't buy it.

👉 The RM900 that started it all

• A Bid Waiver form said the vendor, TT on Tech, would keep last year's price for quarry dust. RM120 per tonne.
• TT on Tech actually charged RM138 per tonne this time. Azrin signed the form anyway.
• Total damage on that one purchase order: RM900. Small money. His signature made it official.

👉 The fake quotes nobody stopped, until someone did

• Company policy required 3 real vendor quotes for every purchase.
• 2 companies that were never registered as vendors kept appearing on bidder lists Azrin approved.
• Neither company had ever been awarded a single purchase order by the company. Not once. He signed off on their quotes anyway 🤦🏻‍♂️

👉 The drug trafficker comparison

• Azrin's whole defence was "I didn't know."
• The court didn't reach for HR case law to test that. It reached for 2 criminal cases involving drug traffickers who claimed they didn't know what was in their bags.
• The ruling: if you deliberately avoid finding out, the law treats you as if you already knew. That's wilful blindness. Not innocence.

9 years counted for nothing once the court decided he chose not to look closely.

He walked away with one month's notice and a small allowance, not the big wrongful dismissal payout you've seen in some of my other case posts.

If you're the one signing off on other people's work, "I didn't check properly" stopped being a defence the moment this award was written.

posts.title: Your AI tool doesn't know the difference between a real regulation and one it invented. And your regulator won't care that it was the AI's fault.
posts.author: Victoria B.
posts.snippet:
Your AI tool doesn't know the difference between a real regulation and one it invented. And your regulator won't care that it was the AI's fault.

That's the accountability gap firms keep walking into. When a hallucinated rule ends up in a client file, "the software made it up" is not a defence - the obligation was always yours.

We've already seen solicitors sanctioned for citing judgments that never existed: invented case names, invented citations, all written in flawless legal English and filed by a real human. It's a predictable failure, not a freak one. A general-purpose AI isn't reading the law — it's predicting the next likely word, with no concept of a source. So it will conjure an MLR threshold or misremember an SRA rule with the same confidence it uses for facts that are true. In an AML assessment or a conveyancing file, that's client detriment, a file that dies in audit, and potentially a reportable event.

Most firms are trying to solve this at the wrong layer asking "which AI tool?" when the real question is about data.

The models that don't hallucinate in production aren't running cleverer prompts. They're grounded - locked to structured, verified, retrievable data so they can only answer from what's real.

That's the thesis why I spend my free time looking into enterprise knowledge graphs feeding GenAI, "designed for reality, proven in production." The knowledge graph is the guardrail: the model retrieves your obligations rather than guessing them. And it's why the unglamorous work of those pulling data out of scattered systems into one clean, queryable place - is quietly the most important compliance-tech decision a firm makes this year. 

You can't ground a model in data you can't reach.

So ask any vendor the only question that matters: where does your answer come from?

If they can't show you a verifiable source behind every output, you haven't bought a compliance aid. You've bought a very articulate liability.

Ground it in your data. Verify the source. Keep a human in the loop.

The firms that win with AI won't be the ones who adopted it fastest. They'll be the ones who fed it the truth.
